s.Students explore how everyday choices af: दैनंदिन निवडींचा दीर्घकालीन परिणामांवर अन्न, आरोग्य, काम, खेळ आणि शिक्षण यांना वेळ प्राधान्य देऊन कसा परिणाम होतो हे विद्यार्थी एक्सप्लोर करतात. चर्चेद्वारे, व्हिज्युअल वेळ-प्राधान्य अक्ष, सर्जनशील सुपरहिरो डिझाइन आणि एक हलकासा तुलनात्मक खेळ, शिकणारे दररोजचे छोटे निर्णय सामर्थ्य, लक्ष केंद्रित आणि भविष्यातील यश कसे निर्माण करतात यावर प्रतिबिंबित करतात.

At this level "where to enter" is already defined by the system; the real question is "what share of my risk budget does this trade take?" Size takes the smallest of three caps: per-trade risk, a fraction of Kelly from your own tested stats, and the room left in portfolio heat. Two longs on two correlated altcoins are, in practice, one bigger long on Bitcoin.

At this level a trade is a hypothesis: "the daily trend is up, price is back at support, and a close below this level proves me wrong." The stop is where the hypothesis dies, the target is the next resistance. You size from the distance between entry and stop, so every trade risks exactly the same {1}–{2}% of capital.

At this level the question isn't whether price goes up, it's "who is trapped and where is the liquidity". You enter when structure (a break or reclaim of a level) and flow (CVD, the change in open interest) agree. Invalidation sits on structure, not on a percentage. And every trade is judged by its expectancy: win rate × R minus loss rate, after fees, funding and slippage.

Bitcoin invites people to ask fundamental questions about money: What gives something value? Why does scarcity matter? How do people agree to exchange? Meeting these ideas early helps learners become thoughtful participants in economic life, able to question prices, understand trade-offs, and recognize that money is a tool people use to coordinate with one another.

Bitcoin is a digital form of money, so understanding the difference between physical and digital systems helps learners ask better questions about how information and value move. Encountering these ideas young builds the confidence to examine new technologies critically, appreciate their possibilities, and consider the responsibilities that come with using them.

Bitcoin is built around time, energy, and shared rules: proof of work connects effort to the security of the network. Young learners do not need to master its technical details yet; they need opportunities to reason about why work has value, why rules matter, and why a patient choice can sometimes lead to a stronger result.
Bitcoin is digital money that no bank or government issues. Transactions are recorded on the blockchain — a public ledger that thousands of computers keep identical copies of.

Each activity ends with an optional, non-evaluative suggested assignment. These are simple ways for learners to connect the session to home: they may share something they made, explain an idea, repeat a small activity, or ask a parent or caregiver a question. No written response, correct answer, or assessment is expected. The aim is simply to extend the conversation and give families a small window into the course.
Each activity follows a consistent format. This allows teachers to quickly identify what is needed and how to run the session effectively.

Each activity has one objective, stated as a single, focused outcome. It defines what students should know, understand, or be able to do by the end of the activity. If time is limited, prioritize the objective over completing every step.

In this activity, learners simulate Bitcoin mining using playing cards as hashes and vocabulary words as transactions. Teams flip cards to find matching pairs. When they find two identical cards, they say “It’s mine.” A valid pair gives them access to the mempool, where they collect one Bitcoin vocabulary word. Words are grouped into blocks and only count after confirmation. The number of cards in the mining pool represents difficulty and is adjusted between rounds. Final scores are calculated by counting the total number of letters in confirmed words stored in each team’s wallet.

In this activity, students take part in a classroom auction using “shells” (or tokens) as a simple form of money. The class runs a live auction where everyday objects are sold one at a time to the highest bidder. As prices emerge in real time, students observe how scarcity (limited items and limited money) and demand (how many people want the same item) shape what something “costs.” A guided reflection links their auction outcomes to core ideas in value, exchange, and price formation, emphasizing that prices are not fixed and that different people value the same object differently.

In this lesson, students construct a story using four independent ideas written on sticky notes. They begin by recalling the earlier story in which Satoshi disappeared and speculate about where he might have gone. Students then generate four ideas from guided prompts and organize them into a beginning, middle, and end structure. Through structured sharing and a sticky note swap, they revise their narratives to include new constraints. The lesson concludes with either a written or illustrated final draft, or a short dramatic role play using a class-generated story arc.

In this whole-class simulation, students roleplay as shipwrecked survivors who must secure essential resources to “survive” a week on a desert island. Using playing cards to represent tools and supplies, learners begin with pure barter, practicing negotiation while encountering common trade barriers such as surplus, scarcity, and the coincidence of wants. A timed “Shell Hunt” then introduces commodity money, as students collect tokens that can be used to simplify exchange. With shells in circulation, the class enters a guided marketplace where students set prices, respond to supply and demand, and experience price discovery. The activity culminates in budgeting and either a short trade round (the {1}-minute core route) or a structured auction (the {2}-minute advanced route) for “treasure” wishlist items, bridging to why money exists.

Money Matters is a classroom economy simulation where each learner operates from a personal Home base. Each student begins with an individual HOME tile displaying their name, challenge card, and financial objective. Learners move through a shared economic system using dice-based movement rules to earn, save, invest, borrow, and trade. The economy is introduced progressively before opening into autonomous role-play, where learners pursue individual goals under shared rules, time constraints, and access limits. Optional extensions allow the system to scale into a richer economy with businesses, infrastructure costs, and education.

Students explore how everyday activities can be grouped into work, rest, and play. Through a shared classification activity and individual routine mapping, learners reflect on how they use their time across a day. The activity builds early awareness of balance, energy, and intentional time use.

Students explore how everyday choices affect long-term outcomes by connecting time preference to food, health, work, play, and education. Through discussion, a visual time-preference axis, creative superhero design, and a lighthearted comparison game, learners reflect on how small daily decisions build strength, focus, and future success.

Students explore how information changes depending on who carries it and who is allowed to hear it. Through a series of short message-passing games with changing rules, learners experience trust, mistakes, and intentional interference firsthand. Reflection focuses on how messages can change, leak, or be protected, and who should decide who gets access to information.

Students explore how their energy changes throughout the day by plotting common activities on a shared class graph and a personal Energy Tracker. By visualizing energy highs and lows across time, learners build early self-awareness about effort, rest, and how energy is spent. This activity lays the foundation for later lessons on time preference, value, and intentional decision-making.
Students explore the concept of time preference through a familiar story,

Students explore the concept of value by identifying everyday items from their own lives and positioning them on a shared visual chart. Through guided discussion and a collaborative wall-based activity, learners compare personal value with price and reflect on how value can change depending on perspective. The activity builds foundational understanding of value, price, and scarcity through discussion, movement, and visual thinking.

Students explore the difference between public and private spaces and information through guided discussion and visual examples. Using familiar everyday situations, learners practice classifying what is usually public or private and reflect on the idea that individuals can choose what information they keep private or share. The activity builds early awareness of privacy, boundaries, and personal responsibility.

Students explore the idea of fairness by participating in a sequence of short games that distribute rewards in different ways. Through direct experience, learners compare unfair systems, random systems, effort-based systems, and Proof of Work. Emotional responses are welcomed and used to support structured reflection. The activity builds a foundational understanding of fairness, reward, and equal opportunity.

Students explore the meaning of price by cutting out everyday items and placing them along a shared price line from cheap to expensive. Through comparison, discussion, and teacher guidance, learners develop a concrete understanding that price is the amount of money something costs and that prices can vary widely between items.
Students find the chest; explain that it will fund one luxury wish each.

Students imagine the future of technology by inventing a new product or system and pitching it in a “Dragons’ Den” format. Learners reflect on how technology evolves, identify real problems to solve, and practice explaining ideas clearly. The activity encourages creativity, critical thinking, and communication while reinforcing the idea that innovation responds to needs over time.

Students leave with stronger financial awareness, critical thinking skills, and a structured understanding of money's evolution. They are not "Bitcoin users." They are prepared learners. When they encounter Bitcoin later in life, they will have the intellectual foundation to understand it responsibly and independently.

Students listen to a teacher-read story in which characters receive rewards that may or may not match their effort. At key moments, the teacher pauses the story to invite discussion and judgment. Learners reflect on fairness, effort, luck, and unequal outcomes, building moral reasoning and vocabulary that supports later lessons on work, reward, and Proof of Work.

Students listen to the story of Satoshi and the Genesis of Bitcoin. Through guided pauses and discussion, they connect the narrative to prior lessons on value, scarcity, time and energy, analogue vs digital systems, and safety and privacy. The teacher uses a printed “white paper” prop to dramatize the moment Satoshi presents his idea to the world. Students reflect on how Bitcoin began as a proposal, required hard work to build, and depends on participants to keep the network alive.
Students map their daily, weekly, or yearly routine, then identify their own work, rest, and play.

Students match older analogue technologies with their modern digital equivalents. Through visual matching, colouring, and discussion, learners explore how tools evolve over time and how innovation changes the way people live, work, and communicate. The activity builds early awareness of technological progress and time-based change.
Students match pairs, colour tools they have used, and circle tools they have at home. Support unfamiliar items.

Students physically position themselves in the classroom to show whether they prefer older or newer technologies. By moving, debating, and explaining their choices, learners compare analogue and digital tools, consider trade-offs, and practice respectful disagreement. The activity reinforces prior learning on technological evolution while increasing engagement through movement.

This chapter brings earlier learning about value, time, energy, choice, and fairness into one shared classroom economy. Students will see that money decisions involve planning, opportunity, risk, and cooperation—and that the same rules can still lead people to different outcomes.

This chapter gathers the ideas from the course—value, scarcity, time and energy, technology, privacy, and shared rules—and connects them to Bitcoin. Learners will meet Bitcoin as a human response to problems with money and as a network maintained by people working together.

This chapter gives young learners a practical starting point for thinking about why people trade, why things matter to different people, and how prices emerge. Students will discover that value is personal, scarcity matters, and a price is not the same thing as what something means to us.

This chapter helps learners notice that time and energy are valuable resources. Students will explore how effort, rest, luck, rules, and patience can shape the rewards people receive, while developing language for fairness and for choices that affect the future.

This chapter introduces the habits of careful digital citizenship: deciding what to share, recognizing who controls access to information, and understanding why private messages deserve protection. Learners will practice making thoughtful choices without being asked to reveal anything personal.

This chapter invites students to become curious observers of the tools around them. By comparing analogue and digital technologies, learners will see that innovation responds to people’s needs, brings trade-offs, and keeps changing the ways we communicate, create, and solve problems.
